item.text: {"chapter_id":"5B","answers":[{"question_id":"5B.1","answer":"The record shows a mixed but predominantly state-led agenda. Sisi formally pursued food security, domestic production, agricultural expansion, private investment, social protection, and state-ownership reform through the 2023 investment council, proposed SOE listings, the World Bank partnership framework, and the budget law (BATCH-0005-E004; BATCH-0006-E005; BATCH-0006-E020; BATCH-0013-E001; BATCH-0019-E012). Some initiatives had implementation evidence, including expanded cash transfers and infrastructure, but many remained announcements or externally supported programs (BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0023-E003). Adverse evidence indicates that military-led megaprojects, debt-financed infrastructure, privileged military and investor access, and weak employment generation displaced broader welfare priorities (BATCH-0005-E009; BATCH-0005-E010; BATCH-0004-E009; BATCH-0009-R10-E001; BATCH-0009-R11-E001). Inflation, poverty, austerity, and inadequate social spending indicate costly outcomes, although COVID-19, the Ukraine war, capital outflows, and global financial conditions materially qualify attribution (BATCH-0008-E004; BATCH-0006-E016; BATCH-0015-E008; BATCH-0019-E010). Sisi's statement that deprivation was an acceptable sacrifice further suggests willingness to privilege development objectives over immediate household welfare, but the extract does not establish intent to pursue private rents in every policy (BATCH-0001-E016).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E004","BATCH-0006-E020","BATCH-0006-E005","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0019-E012","BATCH-0009-R11-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E009","BATCH-0005-E010","BATCH-0004-E009","BATCH-0008-E004","BATCH-0006-E016","BATCH-0015-E008","BATCH-0019-E010","BATCH-0001-E016"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied index provides little executed budget detail or independent evaluation of 2023 policy results.","Direct attribution to Sisi is stronger for announced presidential initiatives than for collective government or externally financed programs."]},{"question_id":"5B.2","answer":"Evidence is insufficient to establish a credible, performance-based system for selecting and retaining economic professionals. The record identifies a presidentially chaired investment council, ministerial and regulatory actions, and trained officials in specialized programs, but does not provide appointment procedures, qualifications, delegated authority, turnover decisions, or performance-based retention evidence (BATCH-0006-E020; BATCH-0008-E007; BATCH-0023-E015). Conversely, broader institutional evidence indicates policymaking was dominated by the presidency, military, and intelligence agencies, with the military favored as a loyal and competent delivery institution rather than independent professional bodies (BATCH-0008-E001; BATCH-0009-R10-E001). The evidence therefore supports operational activity by officials but not a demonstrated meritocratic or independent personnel system.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E020","BATCH-0008-E007","BATCH-0023-E015"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0008-E001","BATCH-0009-R10-E001","BATCH-0009-R10-E002"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No economic-minister appointment records, qualifications, dismissal reasons, or evidence of operational independence are supplied.","Training and institutional activity do not demonstrate selection quality or performance-based accountability."]},{"question_id":"5B.3","answer":"The period reflects substantial macroeconomic instability alongside partial rule-based adjustment. Egypt pursued an IMF program, exchange-rate flexibility, interest-rate increases, SOE reform, and financial-sector measures intended to restore foreign-exchange and fiscal resilience (BATCH-0002-E005; BATCH-0006-E006; BATCH-0006-E005; BATCH-0002-E013). These actions were partly attributable to independent or semi-independent institutions and IMF conditionality rather than Sisi alone (BATCH-0001-E005; BATCH-0022-E013). Outcomes were adverse: the pound lost roughly half its value, inflation approached or exceeded 35–40 percent, debt vulnerability was high, and large debt-service obligations remained (BATCH-0006-E016; BATCH-0007-E020; BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0009-R11-E008). Transparency weaknesses—especially inaccessible military-enterprise debt, omitted allocations, and unpublished audits—undermined fiscal-rule credibility (BATCH-0002-E005; BATCH-0002-E014). The evidence shows crisis adjustment and some formal safeguards, but not sustained compliance with credible rules that protected stability and investment.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E005","BATCH-0006-E006","BATCH-0006-E005","BATCH-0001-E005","BATCH-0022-E013"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E016","BATCH-0007-E020","BATCH-0009-R07-E009","BATCH-0009-R11-E008","BATCH-0002-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index lacks full fiscal accounts, debt-service series, central-bank decision records, and audited execution data.","Causal separation between Sisi's choices, IMF conditions, external shocks, and inherited debt is incomplete."]},{"question_id":"5B.4","answer":"The government adopted several formal measures intended to improve business conditions, including SME-law amendments, investment-council decisions on approvals and golden licenses, SOE listings, competitive-neutrality proposals, recruitment-firm licensing, and regulatory enforcement against Telecom Egypt (BATCH-0003-E006; BATCH-0006-E020; BATCH-0006-E021; BATCH-0009-R04-E003; BATCH-0002-E035). Implementation and outcomes were uneven: many reforms were proposals or lacked follow-through, private-sector competition remained constrained by military dominance, and the private-sector minimum wage lacked binding enforcement (BATCH-0006-E021; BATCH-0009-R11-E009; BATCH-0009-R11-E010; BATCH-0021-E002; BATCH-0021-E004). The World Bank identified longstanding insider privileges and weak employment-generating investment, while women faced much higher unemployment and skills mismatch (BATCH-0004-E009; BATCH-0005-E008). Thus formal rule-making coexisted with unequal enforcement, state privilege, and weak predictability.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E006","BATCH-0006-E020","BATCH-0006-E021","BATCH-0002-E035","BATCH-0009-R04-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-R11-E009","BATCH-0009-R11-E010","BATCH-0021-E002","BATCH-0021-E004","BATCH-0004-E009","BATCH-0005-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index provides few firm-level or sector-level outcome measures for competition, property security, entrepreneurship, or job creation.","Several favorable items document enactment or announcements without implementation verification."]},{"question_id":"5B.5","answer":"The evidence weighs strongly against consistent resistance to economic capture. The government announced competitive-neutrality measures, SOE disclosure and procurement commitments, anti-corruption strategies, and some enforcement actions such as recruitment-license revocations and a Telecom Egypt fine (BATCH-0006-E021; BATCH-0022-E014; BATCH-0004-E001; BATCH-0009-R04-E005; BATCH-0002-E035). However, the Administrative Control Authority lacked credibility and could not monitor military economic activity; military companies remained exempt or opaque, military-led projects operated with autonomy in licensing and contracting, and planned privatization of military companies was repeatedly postponed (BATCH-0002-E004; BATCH-0002-E005; BATCH-0009-R10-E002; BATCH-0009-R10-E004; BATCH-0009-R11-E010). Reports also describe no-bid contracts, privileged land and resource access, and politically connected beneficiaries (BATCH-0005-E010; BATCH-0009-R11-E001). The adverse evidence concerns institutional implementation and repeated non-remedy, although some government-reported disciplinary and licensing actions show limited enforcement capacity (BATCH-0023-E014; BATCH-0009-R04-E005).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E021","BATCH-0022-E014","BATCH-0004-E001","BATCH-0009-R04-E005","BATCH-0002-E035"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0002-E005","BATCH-0009-R10-E002","BATCH-0009-R10-E004","BATCH-0009-R11-E010","BATCH-0005-E010","BATCH-0009-R11-E001","BATCH-0023-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Much evidence is analytical or institutional rather than based on adjudicated contract-level findings.","The index does not identify all beneficiaries or quantify the fiscal effects of favoritism."]},{"question_id":"5B.6","answer":"The record contains real public-investment outputs, including expanded internet and fiber infrastructure, public-transport improvements associated with a reported 4 percent reduction in Greater Cairo air pollution, health-insurance enrollment, cash-transfer systems, World Bank-supported food security, and nuclear-plant construction (BATCH-0002-E033; BATCH-0009-R10-E005; BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0015-E005). There were also substantial plans for new cities, irrigation, desalination, administrative relocation, and transport and digital infrastructure (BATCH-0009-R10-E008; BATCH-0009-R10-E009; BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0019-E003). Yet implementation quality and allocation were contested: megaprojects and military-managed projects consumed large resources, environmental and feasibility studies were absent or inaccessible, power cuts disrupted health and economic activity, and education and health spending remained inadequate (BATCH-0005-E009; BATCH-0009-R10-E009; BATCH-0009-R10-E004; BATCH-0009-R07-E011; BATCH-0008-E004). The evidence supports meaningful infrastructure and administrative capacity gains but not consistently timely, equitable, or high-quality investment.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E033","BATCH-0009-R10-E005","BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0009-R10-E008","BATCH-0019-E001"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E009","BATCH-0009-R10-E009","BATCH-0009-R10-E004","BATCH-0009-R07-E011","BATCH-0008-E004","BATCH-0009-R10-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Many figures are cumulative, planned, externally financed, or officially reported rather than independently audited.","The index lacks consistent project-level cost, completion, utilization, and regional-quality comparisons."]},{"question_id":"5B.7","answer":"The government published budgets, strategies, economic claims, and formal policy documents, participated in IMF, World Bank, UN, and treaty review processes, and created or used bodies for monitoring, evaluation, and reporting (BATCH-0013-E001; BATCH-0005-E001; BATCH-0019-E012; BATCH-0020-E001; BATCH-0020-E002). Some corrective actions occurred, including the presidential pardon of Patrick Zaki, the Telecom Egypt fine, disciplinary proceedings reported by the government, and adjustments to Sinai counterterrorism operations (BATCH-0009-R03-E010; BATCH-0002-E035; BATCH-0023-E014; BATCH-0006-E010). However, official economic claims were not independently verified, military budgets and audits remained opaque, independent monitors faced access restrictions, and external assessments found weak implementation of strategies and little correction after repeated evidence of failure (BATCH-0003-E012; BATCH-0002-E005; BATCH-0009-R10-E004; BATCH-0011-E010; BATCH-0009-R10-E003). The record therefore shows reporting and selective correction, but also denial, restricted scrutiny, and inadequate transparency.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E001","BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0019-E012","BATCH-0020-E001","BATCH-0020-E002","BATCH-0009-R03-E010","BATCH-0002-E035"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E012","BATCH-0002-E005","BATCH-0009-R10-E004","BATCH-0011-E010","BATCH-0009-R10-E003","BATCH-0022-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The candidate index contains few complete audit findings or documented policy reversals tied specifically to economic performance.","Government self-reporting and external criticism often concern different periods or lack shared metrics."]},{"question_id":"5B.8","answer":"Distributional policy was mixed and often inadequate in actual incidence. The government raised public-sector wages, pensions, tax exemptions, cash transfers, minimum wages, farmer debt relief, and social-protection coverage, while Takaful and Karama reached millions of households and disproportionately served women (BATCH-0015-E009; BATCH-0022-E005; BATCH-0022-E006; BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0020-E013). These measures were partly funded and operational, but coverage and adequacy were limited: transfers failed to offset inflation, private and informal workers received weaker protection, real private-sector wages declined, and social spending remained low (BATCH-0022-E013; BATCH-0021-E002; BATCH-0021-E003; BATCH-0009-R07-E010; BATCH-0009-R11-E004). Poverty was concentrated in poorer regions, women faced much higher unemployment, internet access was regionally unequal, and military or investor access to land and resources disadvantaged small farmers and local communities (BATCH-0005-E006; BATCH-0005-E008; BATCH-0002-E034; BATCH-0009-R11-E001). The evidence supports compensatory redistribution but not fair incidence across classes, regions, genders, workers, and marginalized groups.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0015-E009","BATCH-0022-E005","BATCH-0022-E006","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0020-E013"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0022-E013","BATCH-0021-E002","BATCH-0021-E003","BATCH-0009-R07-E010","BATCH-0009-R11-E004","BATCH-0005-E006","BATCH-0005-E008","BATCH-0002-E034","BATCH-0009-R11-E001"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index lacks a complete household-incidence study for 2023 and does not quantify regional or gender effects for every program.","Some coverage figures are government-reported or cumulative and do not establish adequacy or improved living standards."]},{"question_id":"5B.9","answer":"Sisi's government used several shock-response measures: IMF financing and exchange-rate reforms, food-security and bread-subsidy support, expanded cash transfers, wage and tax-relief measures, farmer debt relief, strategic commodity-reserve plans, and electricity and energy-management measures (BATCH-0006-E006; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0022-E005; BATCH-0022-E006; BATCH-0005-E004). Some responses were timely and funded or operational, but targeting and monitoring were weak: inflation reached roughly 35–40 percent, currency depreciation eroded transfers, electricity cuts disrupted vulnerable regions, and IMF reviews were delayed amid unmet transparency conditions (BATCH-0007-E020; BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0009-R07-E011). Government explanations emphasized external shocks, including the Ukraine war, global price rises, higher interest rates, and capital outflows, which materially qualify causal attribution (BATCH-0003-E013; BATCH-0020-E010; BATCH-0019-E010). The record shows active crisis management, but insufficient protection of purchasing power and limited evidence of transparent monitoring or correction.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E006","BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0022-E005","BATCH-0022-E006","BATCH-0005-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0007-E020","BATCH-0009-R07-E009","BATCH-0009-R07-E011","BATCH-0003-E013","BATCH-0020-E010","BATCH-0019-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not provide complete expenditure execution, targeting-error, or monitoring data for the crisis measures.","Several policy effects were still unfolding in 2023, so implementation lags limit outcome attribution."]},{"question_id":"5B.10","answer":"The available evidence does not establish a stronger and more durable economic trajectory by the end of 2023. Positive elements included expanded social-transfer coverage, public-transport and digital infrastructure, health-insurance expansion, lower Sinai violence, and continuing investment in agriculture, energy, and administrative capacity (BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0009-R10-E005; BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0006-E009; BATCH-0002-E033). These gains were accompanied by severe macroeconomic deterioration: high inflation, a halved currency, debt vulnerability, large refinancing needs, declining purchasing power, poverty, weak job creation, and inadequate protection for households (BATCH-0006-E016; BATCH-0007-E017; BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0009-R07-E010; BATCH-0004-E009). Long-term sustainability was further questioned by military dominance, debt-financed megaprojects, opaque contracting, water and environmental pressures, and resource-intensive development choices (BATCH-0005-E009; BATCH-0009-R11-E006; BATCH-0009-R10-E007; BATCH-0009-R10-E014). External shocks and inherited constraints explain part of the deterioration, and some projects had long implementation horizons, but the index does not show that the ruler's choices produced a stronger, fairer, or more resilient trajectory than the inherited baseline.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0009-R10-E005","BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0006-E009","BATCH-0002-E033"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E016","BATCH-0007-E017","BATCH-0009-R07-E009","BATCH-0009-R07-E010","BATCH-0004-E009","BATCH-0005-E009","BATCH-0009-R11-E006","BATCH-0009-R10-E007","BATCH-0009-R10-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The candidate index lacks a fully comparable pre-2014 and end-2023 household-welfare panel.","Several outcomes are cumulative or post-period, and causal attribution is confounded by external shocks, IMF conditions, donor programs, and implementation lags."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["Across the ten lenses, the strongest favorable evidence concerns formal programs, crisis interventions, social-transfer expansion, and selected infrastructure or regulatory outputs.","The strongest adverse evidence concerns macroeconomic deterioration, military and politically connected economic privilege, weak transparency, incomplete implementation, and regressive or inadequate incidence.","Many favorable records are announcements, government claims, or externally supported programs; independent evidence more often documents implementation gaps and household hardship.","Attribution is strongest for presidential announcements, directives, and projects identified as Sisi initiatives, and weaker for collective government, central-bank, IMF, World Bank, military, or subnational actions."]}
